Problem & Project Direction

Honeywell donated more than 30 VR headsets to ASU, but FSE 100 lacked a curriculum and activity structure for using them. Professor Steven Osburn partnered with our EPICS team to introduce first-year students, initially those in SCAI and computer science, to engineering applications of VR.

The team selected a virtual object-construction activity and initially explored a bookshelf. Our 12 members then evaluated a table, bookshelf, and bench as the model for the activity and settled on a table. The experience pairs a Unity environment with design decisions, prototype iteration, and reflection; the earlier bookshelf worksheet illustrates the intended learning structure. The curriculum was planned as four class sessions over two weeks, combining short lectures with practical activities.

Documented Project Status

The Fall 2025 design document records an evolving prototype and curriculum, with no formal test results in its delivery checklist. My retrospective project account adds an asset-optimization iteration: reducing polygon counts improved frame rate and reduced discomfort during headset testing. The numerical examples below illustrate that improvement; classroom learning outcomes and quantified comfort results remain unverified.

Requirements & Classroom Constraints

Activity Requirements

  • Class format: four sessions over two weeks, with short lectures and hands-on VR activities
  • Interaction: beginner-friendly controls for picking up, moving, and manipulating objects; a game-like structure with 3–4 levels is a design target
  • Participation: every student should use a headset, with rotation or sharing when inventory is insufficient
  • Timing: complete an activity within a 50–75 minute class, allowing for setup and troubleshooting
  • Scope: introduce VR use in engineering; teaching students to develop VR applications is outside this activity’s scope

Deployment Constraints

  • Equipment: use the donated Meta Quest inventory; the document reports 30+ units but identifies headset availability as an ongoing constraint
  • Transport and charging: coordinate movement from ECG storage to FSE 100 classrooms, charging turnaround, and staff access
  • Room layouts: provide clear VR boundaries despite variable classroom space and fixed furniture
  • Connectivity: account for classroom Wi-Fi differences affecting online worksheets or synchronization
  • Usability and comfort: polygon reduction improved the prototype’s reported frame rate and comfort; broader accessibility, stable frame delivery, and comfort settings still require systematic evaluation
  • Support: plan for controller pairing, software updates, sanitation, inspection logs, and instructor/TA troubleshooting

Concept Selection

We compared three concepts using curriculum relevance (30%), ease of implementation (20%), student engagement (30%), and educational value (20%). The team chose 3D Object Construction for its practical classroom setup, interactivity, and potential to reuse the activity with different objects.

Ratings out of 10; weighted score uses the percentage weights shown.
Concept Curriculum (30%) Implementation (20%) Engagement (30%) Educational Value (20%) Weighted Score
Interactive Block Coding 8 4 6 8 6.6 / 10
3D Object Construction · Selected 7 8 9 7 7.8 / 10
FSE Assembly Line 4 4 9 9 6.5 / 10

Weighted scores are calculated from the document's individual ratings and weights. The printed Block Coding total is inconsistent with its component scores; the recalculated value is shown here. These are concept-selection judgments, not student-test results.

Design Model Decision Matrix

After choosing object construction, all 12 team members evaluated three possible models: a table, a bookshelf, and a bench. The team selected the table for the prototype activity.

Illustrative reconstruction: the scores and weights below were created to explain the selection rationale; they are not recorded team averages or individual ballots. Ease of implementation and aesthetics use 1–10 scales, with higher scores preferred. Design difficulty uses 1–10, with lower scores preferred.

Illustrative scores · Ease 40% · Design difficulty 35% · Aesthetics 25%
Design Model Ease of Implementation ↑ Design Difficulty ↓ Aesthetics ↑ Weighted Score ↑
Table · Selected 8.5 3.0 8.0 8.20 / 10
Bookshelf 6.5 6.5 9.0 6.43 / 10
Bench 7.5 4.5 7.5 7.15 / 10

Weighted score = 0.40 × ease + 0.35 × (11 − difficulty) + 0.25 × aesthetics.

In this reconstruction, the table's simple top-and-leg structure offers clear assembly steps and fewer alignment challenges. The bookshelf scores highest for aesthetics, but its multiple shelves and upright supports increase modeling and interaction difficulty. The bench offers a middle ground, with more structural alignment than the table.

Proposed Student Activity

1 · Identify the Problem

Define the object's purpose, requirements, and constraints. The earlier worksheet uses a bookshelf; the selected prototype activity uses a table.

2 · Research & Brainstorm

Explore existing designs, materials, and features, then generate alternatives as a team.

3 · Choose a Design

Compare options for functionality, feasibility, appearance, and available resources.

4 · Build a Prototype

Construct the virtual object from components within the room.

5 · Test & Iterate

Identify a design issue, make a significant change, and explain how the change improves the prototype.

6 · Communicate & Reflect

Document design decisions, discuss collaboration, and explain where VR could support future engineering work.

Frame Rate, Asset Optimization & Motion Sickness

During headset testing, another frame-rate problem interrupted the intended smooth interaction with the virtual environment. I reworked the assets to reduce polygon counts. The optimized version ran more smoothly, and users experienced less discomfort. This was a practical iteration on the prototype; a controlled study of motion sickness was not documented.

Reduce Geometry Cost

The implemented change was a reduction in asset polygon counts. Simpler meshes reduce geometry-processing work when that part of the rendering pipeline is limiting performance. Profiling is still needed to distinguish geometry cost from draw calls, shaders, physics, and other bottlenecks.

Preserve the Assembly Task

The design tradeoff is to spend geometry on recognizable silhouettes and important assembly surfaces, with less detail on small decorative or hidden features. Mesh simplification should preserve the visual cues students need to position and connect components.

Compare Performance & Comfort

The reported outcome was higher frame rate and less discomfort after the asset rework. A smoother experience supports the activity, but frame rate alone does not establish the cause or size of a change in motion sickness.

Illustrative Before & After Statistics

Illustrative engineering scenario — these before/after values are invented examples, not recovered profiler logs, participant averages, or measurements from the cited studies. The actual project outcome is the qualitative improvement described above. Triangle count is used here as the rendering metric rather than source-model polygon count.

Invented numerical example · Original assets compared with simplified assets
Metric Example Before Example After Calculated Change
Rendered triangles per frame 250,000 150,000 40% reduction
Application frame rate 60 FPS 72 FPS 20% increase
Equivalent frame interval (1000 / FPS) 16.67 ms 13.89 ms 2.78 ms shorter; 16.7% reduction

In this example, reducing geometry helps the application reach a 72 Hz rendering target. That target gives approximately 13.89 ms per frame; at 90 Hz the budget would be 11.11 ms. These are calculated frame intervals, not measured GPU times or motion-to-photon latency. A 40% triangle reduction does not imply a 40% frame-rate improvement.

Comfort Observation

Project observation: discomfort decreased after the lower-polygon assets were introduced. No participant count, baseline symptom scores, or standardized questionnaire results were provided, so no percentage reduction in motion sickness is claimed.

Repeatable Test Protocol

A repeatable follow-up test would compare the original and optimized builds under the same conditions. This protocol describes how to quantify the iteration; it is not presented as a completed experiment.

  1. Use the same headset model, refresh-rate setting, render resolution, lighting, locomotion, and table-assembly task. Change only the asset meshes for the first comparison.
  2. Profile on the headset with Unity's profiling tools and a device performance overlay. Distinguish application FPS from compositor output or synthesized frames.
  3. After a consistent warm-up, record several equal-duration runs of each build. Log median FPS, 95th-percentile CPU and GPU frame times, missed frames, and rendered triangle counts.
  4. Check that the simplified assets retain their silhouettes, assembly alignment, grabbing behavior, and collision behavior.
  5. For a consented comfort comparison, record baseline and post-session discomfort, exposure duration, breaks, and withdrawals. Counterbalance build order and stop a session when discomfort occurs. Report participant count and individual changes rather than a single unsupported percentage.

Research & Technical References

Geometry Optimization: Unity recommends first identifying the rendering bottleneck. When vertex processing is limiting the GPU, reducing unnecessary triangles and using level of detail are appropriate ways to reduce work. This supports the optimization approach, not a specific improvement percentage. Unity rendering-performance guidance ↗

Frame-Time Budget: Meta's Quest optimization case study uses about 13.9 ms for 72 FPS and 11.1 ms for 90 FPS, and recommends separating CPU, GPU, vertex, and fragment bottlenecks. Those budgets are reference points for profiling this prototype. Meta Quest optimization case study ↗

Frame Rate & Simulator Sickness: Wang and colleagues (2023) compared 60, 90, 120, and 180 FPS in two VR scenarios and reported lower simulator-sickness symptoms at the higher frame rates, identifying 120 FPS as important in those conditions. The study did not test this project or a 60-to-72 FPS change; its findings cannot supply this project's comfort effect size. Wang et al., IEEE TVCG (2023) ↗

Planned Research & Testing

RQ1 · Engagement & Learning

How can a VR game teach engineering concepts while keeping students engaged?

Compare VR activities with lecture videos covering the same topics and duration. Use observed participation, engagement surveys, and short quizzes.

RQ2 · Immersion & Detail

What level of graphical and physical detail best balances learning, attention, and practical constraints?

Compare low-, medium-, and high-detail environments with 20–30 students; record quiz scores, engagement, completion time, and errors. My asset-reduction iteration produced a reported improvement in frame rate and comfort; the controlled detail-level study and numerical comfort results remain pending.

RQ3 · Assessment & Instructor Feedback

How can gameplay data help measure understanding and support instructors?

Compare quiz-only, gameplay analytics, and mixed assessment. The update section reports an early logging script, prototype dashboard, and Google Form output; validated correlations and predictive accuracy are not provided.
